claim: The dopamine transporter (DAT), the norepinephrine transporter (NET), and the serotonin transporter (SERT) are members of the solute carrier six (SLC6) family.
source: The dopamine transporter (DAT), the norepinephrine transporter (NET), and the serotonin transporter (SERT) are members of the solute carrier six (SLC6) family.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and is supported by citation to Kristensen et al., 2011.

claim: DAT, NET, and SERT mediate reuptake of released dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, respectively.
source: DAT, NET, and SERT mediate reuptake of released dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, respectively (Kristensen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Kristensen et al., 2011.

claim: DAT, NET, and SERT terminate monoaminergic signaling by reuptake.
source: By this action, they terminate monoaminergic signaling and—in concert with the vesicular monoamine transporters—replenish vesicular stores.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: DAT, NET, and SERT replenish vesicular stores in concert with vesicular monoamine transporters.
source: By this action, they terminate monoaminergic signaling and—in concert with the vesicular monoamine transporters—replenish vesicular stores.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: DAT, NET, and SERT are secondary active transporters.
source: These transporters are secondary active in nature; they utilize the free energy contained in the transmembrane Na+ gradient (established by the Na+/K+ pump) to drive concentrative monoamine uptake into cells in which they are expressed (Burtscher et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Burtscher et al., 2019.

claim: DAT, NET, and SERT utilize the free energy contained in the transmembrane Na+ gradient to drive concentrative monoamine uptake.
source: These transporters are secondary active in nature; they utilize the free energy contained in the transmembrane Na+ gradient (established by the Na+/K+ pump) to drive concentrative monoamine uptake into cells in which they are expressed (Burtscher et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Burtscher et al., 2019.

claim: The transmembrane Na+ gradient is established by the Na+/K+ pump.
source: These transporters are secondary active in nature; they utilize the free energy contained in the transmembrane Na+ gradient (established by the Na+/K+ pump) to drive concentrative monoamine uptake into cells in which they are expressed (Burtscher et al., 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Burtscher et al., 2019.

claim: SLC6 transporters have been postulated to operate via the alternate access mechanism.
source: SLC6 transporters have been postulated to operate via the alternate access mechanism (Jardetzky, 1966): they undergo a closed loop of partial reactions constituting a complete transport cycle (Rudnick and Sandtner, 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Jardetzky, 1966 and Rudnick and Sandtner, 2019.

claim: SLC6 transporters undergo a closed loop of partial reactions constituting a complete transport cycle.
source: SLC6 transporters have been postulated to operate via the alternate access mechanism (Jardetzky, 1966): they undergo a closed loop of partial reactions constituting a complete transport cycle (Rudnick and Sandtner, 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Rudnick and Sandtner, 2019.

claim: The partial reactions of the transport cycle require conformational rearrangements and binding/unbinding of substrate and co-substrate ions.
source: These partial reactions require conformational rearrangements and binding/unbinding of substrate and co-substrate ions.
evidence: This is directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Crystal structures obtained from the prokaryotic homolog LeuT, Drosophila DAT, and human SERT support the general concept of alternate access.
source: It is gratifying to note that crystal structures obtained from the prokaryotic homolog LeuT, Drosophila DAT, and human SERT itself support the general concept of alternate access (Yamashita et al., 2005; Penmatsa et al., 2013; Coleman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Yamashita et al., 2005; Penmatsa et al., 2013; Coleman et al., 2016.

claim: SERT and DAT are closely related as revealed by crystal structures.
source: These crystal structures also reveal SERT and DAT to be closely related.
evidence: This is directly stated in the introduction.

claim: The root mean square deviation between the outward-facing structure of human SERT and Drosophila DAT differs by only approximately 1 Å.
source: This is evident from the root mean square deviation, which differs by only approximately 1 Å between the outward-facing structure of human SERT and Drosophila DAT.
evidence: This is directly stated in the introduction.

claim: DAT, NET, and SERT share a rich and partially overlapping pharmacology.
source: DAT, NET, and SERT also share a rich and partially overlapping pharmacology (Sitte and Freissmuth, 2015): there are many drugs that inhibit transporter function by either blocking or inducing reverse transport.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Sitte and Freissmuth, 2015.

claim: Many drugs inhibit DAT, NET, and SERT function by either blocking or inducing reverse transport.
source: DAT, NET, and SERT also share a rich and partially overlapping pharmacology (Sitte and Freissmuth, 2015): there are many drugs that inhibit transporter function by either blocking or inducing reverse transport.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Sitte and Freissmuth, 2015.

claim: The mechanisms of blocking or inducing reverse transport account for therapeutics used for the treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: These mechanisms account for therapeutics used for the treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders (major depression, general anxiety disorder, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder) and for many illicit drugs that are psychoactive and abused (Hasenhuetl et al., 2019; Niello et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Hasenhuetl et al., 2019; Niello et al., 2020.

claim: The transport stoichiometry of SERT is considered to be electroneutral.
source: Despite the similarity in structure and function, the three transporters differ in many more aspects than just ligand recognition: the transport stoichiometry of SERT and DAT/NET is considered to be electroneutral and electrogenic, respectively.

claim: The transport stoichiometry of DAT/NET is considered to be electrogenic.
source: Despite the similarity in structure and function, the three transporters differ in many more aspects than just ligand recognition: the transport stoichiometry of SERT and DAT/NET is considered to be electroneutral and electrogenic, respectively.

claim: The crystal structure of both hSERT and dDAT shows two bound Na+ ions.

claim: Only one Na+ ion is thought to be released on the intracellular side in both SERT and DAT.

claim: Cl- plays a modulatory role in the transport cycle of SERT and DAT.

claim: Cl- is not essential for the transport stoichiometry of SERT and DAT.

claim: SERT antiports intracellular K+.

source: Currents through SERT (amplitudes of which are represented as diamond symbols in Figure 3L and square symbols in Figure 6C) are completely uncoupled from the catalytic transporter cycle; in spite of its electroneutral stoichiometry, SERT mediates an inwardly directed current, which is eliminated by removal of Kin+ (circle symbols in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SERT mediates an inwardly directed current, which is eliminated by removal of intracellular K+.
source: Currents through SERT (amplitudes of which are represented as diamond symbols in Figure 3L and square symbols in Figure 6C) are completely uncoupled from the catalytic transporter cycle; in spite of its electroneutral stoichiometry, SERT mediates an inwardly directed current, which is eliminated by removal of Kin+ (circle symbols in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6C, and supported by citations to Schicker et al., 2012; Hasenhuetl et al., 2016.

claim: The catalytic rates of DAT in the presence or absence of intracellular K+ are very similar.

claim: The catalytic rates of NET in the presence or absence of intracellular K+ are very similar.
source: As shown in Figure 6E and F, the catalytic rates of DAT and NET in the presence or absence of Kin+ are very similar.
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: SERT shows an approximately twofold deceleration in the catalytic rate in the absence of intracellular K+ when compared to its recovery rate in the presence of high intracellular K+.

claim: High intracellular Na+ accelerated the recovery of all three transporters.

claim: All monoamine transporters can bind intracellular K+.

evidence: This is directly stated as a hypothesis to explain the data.

claim: Bound intracellular K+ is released on the intracellular side prior to the return step by DAT and NET.
source: The data, represented in Figure 6, can be explained by a model that posits that all monoamine transporters can bind Kin+, but that the bound Kin+ is released on the intracellular side prior to the return step by DAT and NET.
evidence: This is directly stated as a hypothesis to explain the data.

claim: Intracellular K+ is released on the extracellular side after being antiported by SERT.
source: In contrast, Kin+ is released on the extracellular side after being antiported by SERT.
evidence: This is directly stated as a hypothesis to explain the data.

claim: The kinetic model for DAT by Erreger et al., 2008 was used as a starting point for modeling DAT and NET.
source: As a starting point for modeling DAT and NET, we used the previously proposed kinetic model for DAT by Erreger et al., 2008, shaded in grey in Figure 7A, which is nested within our proposed model.
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 7A, with citation to Erreger et al., 2008.

claim: The kinetic models could faithfully reproduce the experimental finding that only APP+ uptake by SERT was voltage-independent.

claim: The kinetic models could faithfully reproduce the experimental finding that the removal of intracellular K+ abrogated the steady-state current only in SERT but not in DAT.
source: (ii) the removal of Kin+ abrogated the steady-state current only in SERT but not in DAT (Figure 7F, G and Figure 6A, C);
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 7F, G compared to Figure 6A, C.

claim: The kinetic models could faithfully reproduce the experimental finding that the removal of intracellular K+ did not slow down the return of DAT and NET from the inward- to the outward-facing conformation, while it reduced this rate in SERT by twofold.
source: (iii) the removal of Kin+ did not slow down the return of DAT and NET from the inward- to the outward-facing conformation, while it reduced this rate in SERT by twofold (Figure 6E–G to Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6E-G compared to Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The differences in handling of intracellular K+ incorporated into the model are necessary and sufficient to account for the differences in the forward transport mode of DAT, NET, and SERT.
source: This indicates that the underlying assumptions are valid and allow for a reasonable approximation, which has explanatory power: the differences in handling of Kin+ incorporated into the model are necessary and sufficient to account for the differences in the forward transport mode of DAT, NET, and SERT.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: APP+ is a fluorescent analog of MPP+.
source: One such fluorescent substrate is APP+, a fluorescent analog of MPP+, a neurotoxin that targets monoaminergic neurons (Javitch et al., 1985; Pifl et al., 1991).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Javitch et al., 1985; Pifl et al., 1991.

claim: MPP+ is a neurotoxin that targets monoaminergic neurons.
source: One such fluorescent substrate is APP+, a fluorescent analog of MPP+, a neurotoxin that targets monoaminergic neurons (Javitch et al., 1985; Pifl et al., 1991).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Javitch et al., 1985; Pifl et al., 1991.

claim: APP+ is taken up by cells expressing DAT, NET, and SERT.

evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Solis et al., 2012; Karpowicz et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2014.

claim: All major differences between DAT, NET, and SERT can be accounted for by the distinct handling of intracellular K+.
source: It is evident that DAT and NET resemble SERT in most aspects. We show here that all major differences can be accounted for by the distinct handling of Kin+.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: In SERT, physiological intracellular K+ concentrations accelerated the rate of substrate uptake; it was twofold faster than in the absence of intracellular K+.
source: (i) in SERT, physiological Kin+ concentrations accelerated the rate of substrate uptake; it was twofold faster than in the absence Kin+ (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: DAT and NET returned to the outward-facing state with the same rate regardless of whether intracellular K+ was present or not.
source: In contrast, DAT and NET returned to the outward-facing state with the same rate regardless of whether Kin+was present or not (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Intracellular K+ did not affect the rate of substrate uptake by DAT and NET.
source: Accordingly, Kin+ did not affect the rate of substrate uptake by DAT and NET (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The catalytic rate of SERT was independent of voltage in the presence of physiological ionic gradients.
source: (ii) The catalytic rate of SERT was independent of voltage in the presence of physiological ionic gradients (Figure 3L and Figure 5L).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 3L and Figure 5L.

claim: The catalytic rate of DAT was voltage-dependent.
source: This was not the case for DAT and NET (Figure 3J and K and Figure 5J and K, respectively).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 3J and Figure 5J.

claim: The catalytic rate of NET was voltage-dependent.
source: This was not the case for DAT and NET (Figure 3J and K and Figure 5J and K, respectively).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 3K and Figure 5K.

claim: In all three transporters, release of intracellular Na+ from the inward-facing conformation was electrogenic.
source: (iii) In all three transporters, release of Nain+ from the inward-facing conformation was electrogenic.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: In SERT, electrogenic intracellular Na+ dissociation was canceled out by electrogenic intracellular K+ binding to the inward-open empty transporter and its subsequent antiport.
source: In SERT, this electrogenic Nain+ dissociation was canceled out by electrogenic Kin+ binding to the inward-open empty transporter and its subsequent antiport, thereby rendering the cycle completion rate voltage-independent.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: In DAT and NET, the cycle completion rate remained voltage-dependent despite the fact that intracellular K+ also bound in a voltage-dependent manner.
source: In DAT and NET, however, the cycle completion rate remained voltage-dependent despite the fact that Kin+ also bound in a voltage-dependent manner.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: The steady current component carried by the electroneutral SERT was produced by an uncoupled Na+ flux through a channel state that was in equilibrium with the intracellular K+-bound inward-facing conformation.
source: The steady current component carried by the electroneutral SERT was produced by an uncoupled Na+ flux through a channel state that was in equilibrium with the Kin+-bound inward-facing conformation (Schicker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Schicker et al., 2012.

claim: DAT-mediated transport was accompanied by the translocation of coupled net positive charges in each cycle.
source: DAT-mediated transport was accompanied by the translocation of coupled net positive charges in each cycle.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: DAT-mediated steady-state currents were originally modeled to be strictly coupled to substrate transport.
source: Thus, DAT-mediated steady-state currents were originally modeled to be strictly coupled to substrate transport (Erreger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Erreger et al., 2008.

claim: DAT carries an uncoupled current component.
source: However, our data suggest that DAT also carries a previously suggested uncoupled current component (Sonders et al., 1997; Sitte et al., 1998; Carvelli et al., 2004), which adds to those associated with DAT-mediated ionic transport.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Sonders et al., 1997; Sitte et al., 1998; Carvelli et al., 2004.

claim: The uncoupled current in DAT is contingent on the presence of intracellular K+.
source: This uncoupled current in DAT, just like in SERT, is contingent on the presence of intracellular Kin+.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: Binding of intracellular K+ to DAT at the Na2 site was proposed by a study that employed extensive molecular dynamic simulations.

claim: The amino acids that co-ordinate and form the Na2 site are absolutely conserved in all three plasmalemmal monoamine transporters.
source: The amino acids that co-ordinate and form the Na2 site are absolutely conserved in all three plasmalemmal monoamine transporters (Penmatsa et al., 2013; Coleman et al., 2016; Cheng and Bahar, 2019).

claim: In SERT, Na+ binding to Na2 site is thought to trigger conformational transitions essential for physiological substrate transport.
source: In SERT, Na+ binding to Na2 site is thought to trigger conformational transitions essential for physiological substrate transport (Felts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Felts et al., 2014.

claim: Dissociation of Na+ from the Na2 site leads to water flux from the cytosol that promotes transition of the transporter into the inward-facing conformation and subsequent substrate dissociation on the intracellular side.
source: Dissociation of Na+ from the Na2 site, in turn, leads to water flux from the cytosol that promotes transition of the transporter into the inward-facing conformation and subsequent substrate dissociation on the intracellular side (Cheng and Bahar, 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Cheng and Bahar, 2019.

claim: The voltage dependence of peak amplitudes is identical in the presence of high intracellular Na+ and high intracellular K+ in all three plasmalemmal monoamine transporters.

claim: Intracellular K+ and intracellular Na+ binding occurs at the Na2 site in a mutually exclusive manner.
source: these observations support the conjecture that Kin+ and Nain+ binding occurs at the Na2 site in a mutually exclusive manner.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation for all differences between SERT, NET, and DAT is that intracellular K+ is antiported by SERT but not by DAT and NET.
source: The most parsimonious explanation for all differences between SERT, NET, and DAT was to posit that Kin+ is antiported by SERT but not by DAT and NET.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: All three transporters carry a negative charge through the membrane on return from the substrate-free inward- to the substrate-free outward-facing conformation.
source: All three transporters carry a negative charge through the membrane on return from the substrate-free inward- to the substrate-free outward-facing conformation (presumably a negatively charged amino-acid).
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: In SERT, the charge on the transporter is neutralized by the counter-transported intracellular K+.
source: In the case of SERT, however, the charge on the transporter is neutralized by the counter-transported Kin+.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: The return step is slow and therefore rate-limiting in SERT.
source: Because the return step is slow and therefore rate-limiting, it determines the voltage dependence of substrate uptake.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: The intracellular K+-binding site in SERT can alternatively accept protons.

evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Keyes and Rudnick, 1982.

claim: Protons—as an alternative co-substrate that is antiported—support the return step from the inward- to the outward-facing substrate-free conformation in SERT.
source: Hence protons—as an alternative co-substrate that is antiported—support the return step from the inward- to the outward-facing substrate-free conformation (Hasenhuetl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Hasenhuetl et al., 2016.

claim: In the absence of intracellular K+, DAT and NET transporters return from the substrate-free inward- to the substrate-free outward-facing conformation.
source: However, this can be refuted for DAT and NET for the following reasons: the presence or absence of Kin+ did not change their catalytic rates (Figure 6E and F). Thus, in the absence of Kin+, the transporters seem to return from the substrate-free inward- to the substrate-free outward-facing conformation.
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Protons cannot be antiported by DAT.
source: Additionally, H+ failed to accelerate the catalytic rate of DAT (data not shown) and the slope of the IV curve for the peak current remained steep (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). These observations indicate that protons (like Kin+) cannot be antiported by DAT.

claim: APP+ is a full substrate of DAT.
source: Interestingly, APP+ is a full substrate of DAT: the currents, which were elicited by APP+, were indistinguishable to those induced by the cognate substrate dopamine and other full substrates such as D-amphetamine (Erreger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Erreger et al., 2008.

claim: APP+ is a poor substrate for SERT.
source: Taken together these observations, APP+ is a poor substrate for SERT: its actions can be rationalized by assuming that it traps transporters in one or several conformational intermediates, which are exited with a rate slower than the return step.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: APP+ had similar KM values for DAT and SERT.
source: Therefore, DAT and SERT diverge in their handling of APP+: while APP+ had similar KM values for DAT and SERT, the catalytic rate of the transport cycle was equivalent to that of the cognate substrate in DAT, but substantially lower in SERT.

claim: The catalytic rate of the transport cycle for APP+ was equivalent to that of the cognate substrate in DAT.
source: Therefore, DAT and SERT diverge in their handling of APP+: while APP+ had similar KM values for DAT and SERT, the catalytic rate of the transport cycle was equivalent to that of the cognate substrate in DAT, but substantially lower in SERT.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: The catalytic rate of the transport cycle for APP+ was substantially lower than that of the cognate substrate in SERT.
source: Therefore, DAT and SERT diverge in their handling of APP+: while APP+ had similar KM values for DAT and SERT, the catalytic rate of the transport cycle was equivalent to that of the cognate substrate in DAT, but substantially lower in SERT.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: NET expressed in HEK293 cells was originally reported to support both a peak and a steady current when challenged with a substrate.
source: Originally, NET expressed in HEK293 cells was reported to support both a peak and a steady current, when challenged with a substrate (Galli et al., 1995; Sommerauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Galli et al., 1995; Sommerauer et al., 2012.

claim: In the present study, only the peak current was observed with the superfusion system for NET.
source: However, in the present study, we only observed the peak current with our superfusion system, which allowed for a rapid exchange of solutions: neither APP+ nor the cognate substrate norepinephrine elicited a steady current.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: The absence of the steady current in NET can be attributed to the very slow catalytic rate of NET.
source: The absence of the steady current can be attributed to the very slow catalytic rate of NET: it is evident that NET, in contrast to DAT and SERT, returns on a timescale of seconds from the inward- to the outward-facing state.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: NET dwells in the inward-facing state with a lifetime of τ = ~7 s.
source: NET dwells in the inward-facing state with a lifetime of τ = ~7 s (Figure 6F), which is >10–20 times longer than the dwell time of DAT and SERT (DAT, τ = ~0.3 s; SERT, τ = ~0.6 s; Figure 6E and G).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: DAT dwells in the inward-facing state with a lifetime of τ = ~0.3 s.
source: NET dwells in the inward-facing state with a lifetime of τ = ~7 s (Figure 6F), which is >10–20 times longer than the dwell time of DAT and SERT (DAT, τ = ~0.3 s; SERT, τ = ~0.6 s; Figure 6E and G).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: SERT dwells in the inward-facing state with a lifetime of τ = ~0.6 s.
source: NET dwells in the inward-facing state with a lifetime of τ = ~7 s (Figure 6F), which is >10–20 times longer than the dwell time of DAT and SERT (DAT, τ = ~0.3 s; SERT, τ = ~0.6 s; Figure 6E and G).
evidence: This is directly stated and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Turnover numbers determined by maximal uptake rates divided by maximal binding sites were reported as five times lower in NET than in DAT expressed in COS-7 and human neuroblastoma cells.
source: Turnover numbers determined by maximal uptake rates divided by maximal binding sites were also reported as five times lower in NET than in DAT expressed in COS-7 and human neuroblastoma cells (Pifl et al., 1996).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Pifl et al., 1996.

claim: The very slow turnover of NET explains the absence of coupled or uncoupled NET-mediated currents in spite of the proposed electrogenic stoichiometry.
source: Thus, this very slow turnover explains the absence of coupled or uncoupled NET-mediated currents in spite of the proposed electrogenic stoichiometry (Gu et al., 1996).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Gu et al., 1996.

claim: In SERT, the binding site for intracellular K+ remains intact upon conversion of the transporter from the inward- to the outward-facing conformation.
source: Our analysis provides a unifying concept of substrate transport through all three monoamine transporters, that is, they are equivalent in all aspects of their transport cycle but one: in SERT, the binding site for Kin+ remains intact upon conversion of the transporter from the inward- to the outward-facing conformation.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: In DAT and NET, the binding site for intracellular K+ is less stable than in SERT.
source: In contrast, this binding site is less stable in DAT and NET.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: The loss in affinity of the intracellular K+ binding site leads to the shedding of intracellular K+ prior to the return step in DAT and NET.
source: The resulting loss in affinity leads to the shedding of Kin+ prior to the return step.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: If DAT and NET do not antiport intracellular K+, their concentrative power must be independent of the existing K+ gradient across the plasma membrane.
source: If DAT and NET do not antiport Kin+, its concentrative power must be independent of the existing K+ gradient across the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is directly stated as a logical consequence.

claim: If the stoichiometry of DAT and NET is electrogenic, a change in membrane voltage is predicted to increase or decrease substrate uptake at steady state depending on the direction of the voltage change.
source: On the other hand, if the stoichiometry of DAT and NET is electrogenic, a change in membrane voltage is predicted to increase or decrease substrate uptake at steady state depending on the direction of the voltage change.
evidence: This is directly stated as a prediction.

claim: All three monoamine transporters can transport substrate in the absence of intracellular K+.
source: However, steady-state assessment of transporter-mediated substrate uptake is hindered by the fact that all three monoamine transporters can also transport substrate in the absence of Kin+.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: DAT and NET are less likely than SERT to antiport intracellular K+.
source: Based on our data we conclude that DAT and NET are less likely than SERT to antiport Kin+, because we cannot rule out that they can occasionally carry the Kin+ ion through the membrane.

claim: SERT antiports intracellular K+ in the majority of its cycles but may return empty in some instances.
source: Conversely, SERT antiports Kin+ in the majority of its cycles but may return empty in some instances.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: The differences between DAT, NET, and SERT with respect to their handling of intracellular K+ represent a continuum, as opposed to divergence, in ionic coupling and kinetic decision points during substrate transport.
source: We thus believe that the differences between these three transporters with respect to their handling of Kin+ represent a continuum, as opposed to divergence, in ionic coupling and kinetic decision points during substrate transport.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: The family of SLC1 glutamate transporters comprises members that are categorized as either K+-dependent or K+-independent.
source: In this context, it is worth pointing out that the family of SLC1 glutamate transporters, another important family of neurotransmitter transporters, comprises members that are categorized as either (i) K+-dependent, that is, they utilize Kin+ as an obligatory co-substrate or (ii) K+-independent, that is, they do not require Kin+ for completion of the transport cycle (Alleva and Machtens, 2021).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Alleva and Machtens, 2021.

claim: Intracellular K+ was shown to bind to the same binding sites in both K+-dependent and K+-independent subfamilies of SLC1 glutamate transporters.
source: However, Kin+ was shown to bind to the same binding sites in both subfamilies (Wang et al., 2019; Kortzak et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Wang et al., 2019; Kortzak et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The presence of intracellular K+ is not obligatory for any representative of the monoamine transporters.

claim: The differences in intracellular K+ handling by SERT and by DAT and NET may have a distinct physiological impact and may have arisen due to evolutionary optimization and adaptation to physiological requirements.
source: The differences in Kin+ handling by SERT and by DAT and NET and concomitant differences in voltage-dependence profiles may have a distinct physiological impact and may have arisen due to evolutionary optimization and adaptation to physiological requirements.
evidence: This is directly stated as a speculation.

claim: SERT is the most divergent member of the three monoamine transporters based on alignment of primary sequences.
source: An analysis based on the alignment of the primary sequences of DAT, NET, and SERT reveals that SERT is the most divergent member of the three monoamine transporters.
evidence: This is directly stated in the discussion.

claim: SERT is expressed in both neurons and non-excitable cells, for example, in the trophoblast of the placenta.
source: SERT is expressed, in both neurons and non-excitable cells, for example, in the trophoblast of the placenta (Balkovetz et al., 1989; Kliman et al., 2018; Rudnick and Sandtner, 2019).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Balkovetz et al., 1989; Kliman et al., 2018; Rudnick and Sandtner, 2019.

claim: The membrane potential in cells expressing SERT can range from at least 0 mV to −84 mV, with further variations under different biological processes.
source: The membrane potential in these cells can range from at least 0 mV to −84 mV, with further variations under different biological processes (Carstensen et al., 1973; Friedhoff and Sonenberg, 1983; Greenwood et al., 1996; Birdsey et al., 1997; Kirby et al., 2003).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Carstensen et al., 1973; Friedhoff and Sonenberg, 1983; Greenwood et al., 1996; Birdsey et al., 1997; Kirby et al., 2003.

claim: The voltage independence of SERT is an evolutionary adaptation to maintain effective forward transport over a large variation in membrane potential.
source: It is, therefore, conceivable that the voltage independence of SERT is an evolutionary adaptation to maintain effective forward transport over a large variation in membrane potential.
evidence: This is directly stated as a speculation.

claim: DAT has been previously predicted to exploit membrane hyperpolarization caused by activated autoreceptors and open G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channel to augment dopamine reuptake and synaptic clearance.
source: DAT, on the other hand, has been previously predicted to exploit membrane hyperpolarization caused by activated autoreceptors and open G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channel to augment dopamine reuptake and synaptic clearance (Sonders et al., 1997).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Sonders et al., 1997.

claim: There is a trade-off in plasmalemmal monoamine transporter function.
source: Hence, there seems to be a trade-off in plasmalemmal monoamine transporter function.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: SERT operates in the forward transport mode with a constant rate regardless of membrane potential.
source: Because of electrogenic binding and subsequent counter-transport of Kin+, SERT operates in the forward transport mode with a constant rate regardless of membrane potential, but it cannot exploit the membrane potential to fuel its concentrative power.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: SERT cannot exploit the membrane potential to fuel its concentrative power.
source: Because of electrogenic binding and subsequent counter-transport of Kin+, SERT operates in the forward transport mode with a constant rate regardless of membrane potential, but it cannot exploit the membrane potential to fuel its concentrative power.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: DAT and NET can harvest the energy of the transmembrane potential to fuel their concentrative power.
source: In contrast, DAT and NET can harvest the energy of the transmembrane potential to fuel its concentrative power.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.

claim: The substrate uptake rate of DAT and NET is voltage-dependent and strongly reduced or increased upon membrane depolarization or hyperpolarization, respectively.
source: As a trade-off, the substrate uptake rate of DAT and NET is voltage-dependent and strongly reduced or increased upon membrane depolarization or hyperpolarization, respectively.
evidence: This is directly stated as a conclusion.
